title: Elaine's Electric Shocks
text:
Do people ever help purely for the sake of the other person, or always, in the end, to ease their own discomfort? In 1981 C. Daniel Batson and his colleagues at the University of Kansas designed an experiment to test this.

Female students watched, over what they believed was closed-circuit television, as another young woman named Elaine took part in a learning task in which she received mild electric shocks. In fact Elaine was a confederate and the scene was recorded. As the trials went on, Elaine reacted badly and explained that she had had a frightening experience with electricity as a child. The experimenter then asked the observer whether she would be willing to take Elaine's place for the rest of the session.

Two things were varied. Some observers were led to feel strong empathy for Elaine, for example by learning that she shared their values and interests. And some were told they could leave after watching just two trials, while others would have to watch all ten. If people helped only to escape the distress of watching, the easy exit should have reduced helping. That is what happened among low-empathy observers. But high-empathy observers offered to trade places at high rates even when they could easily have walked away.
lesson: Real empathy moves people to help even when looking away would be easier. Taking time to understand someone's situation is often the first step to caring for them.
people: C. Daniel Batson, Bruce Duncan, Paula Ackerman, Terese Buckley, Kimberly Birch
source: Batson, C. D., Duncan, B. D., Ackerman, P., Buckley, T., and Birch, K. (1981). Is empathic emotion a source of altruistic motivation? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 40(2), 290-302.
